time_prose: Late September, over several days around the autumnal equinox.
origin: The shrine's principal annual festival, re-enacting the consolation of Michizane's spirit.
meaning: To comfort the enshrined kami and pray for peace and learning.
ritual: A grand procession bears the divine palanquin (o-mikoshi) through the town in Heian-style costume.
prayer: For scholarship, and for the repose and favor of Tenjin.
visitor_notes: The costumed evening procession is the highlight; the approach fills with festival stalls.

time_prose: The first Day of the Horse (hatsuuma) of the second lunar month — usually in February. Date varies each year.
origin: Commemorates the descent of the Inari deity onto Inariyama on the first Day of the Horse in 711.
meaning: A petition for a bountiful year and prosperous business, the most important rite of the Inari calendar.
ritual: Worshippers receive shirushi-no-sugi (a blessed cedar sprig); the mountain fills with pilgrims through the night.
prayer: For abundant harvest and flourishing trade.
visitor_notes: Among the busiest days of the year at the shrine; expect dense crowds on the lower paths.

origin: The shrine's principal annual rite, historically tied to the imperial court's recognition of Hikawa as the ichinomiya of Musashi.
meaning: Thanksgiving and petition for the peace and prosperity of the region.
ritual: Formal offerings (shinsen), kagura dance, and the dispatch of an imperial envoy in recognition of the shrine's chokusaisha status.
prayer: For regional peace and bountiful harvests.
visitor_notes: Ceremonies are largely formal; the approach and grounds are open to visitors.

time_prose: The 10th lunar month (Kamiarizuki) — in 2026, late November. Dates set annually by the lunar calendar.
origin: When the myriad gods of Japan are believed to leave their own shrines and gather at Izumo to deliberate on human affairs and relationships.
meaning: A solemn reception of the assembled deities and a petition for auspicious bonds in the coming year.
ritual: The Karasade rites welcome and later send off the gods; the shrine observes strict quiet during the divine assembly.
prayer: For good relationships and fortunate unions.
visitor_notes: The most spiritually charged period at Izumo; visitors are asked to keep a reverent quiet during the rites.

time_prose: Late April to early May, around the Showa Day holiday.
origin: An annual rite honoring the enshrined spirits, paired with public performances of classical arts.
meaning: Thanksgiving and prayer for the peace and prosperity of the nation.
ritual: Court music (gagaku), bugaku dance, noh, and yabusame horseback archery are offered before the deities.
prayer: For national peace and the people's wellbeing.
visitor_notes: The traditional-arts offerings are free to watch on the festival grounds.

time_prose: Throughout July; Yamaboko Junko float processions on July 17 (Saki Matsuri) and July 24 (Ato Matsuri).
origin: Originated in 869 as a goryo-e rite to dispel a nationwide epidemic, sending 66 halberds to the Shinsen-en garden for the provinces of Japan.
meaning: A purification of the city and a petition for protection from pestilence and disaster.
ritual: Mikoshi processions, the towering yamaboko floats, and the Yamaboko Junko parade through central Kyoto.
prayer: For freedom from disease and disaster.
visitor_notes: The float processions on the 17th and 24th draw large crowds; arrive early along Shijo-dori.
